name: DTVM (ZetaEngine lazy-JIT Wasm VM)
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift); also Wasmer Singlepass, Cranelift and LLVM
metric: startup (time to first invocation) and latency (processing time = load+compile+execute)
workload: PolyBench/C 4.2.1 (30 kernels, SMALL_DATASET, compiled to Wasm with wasi-sdk clang -O3), 21 WAPM packages and a recursive Fibonacci(30) / integer-overflow contract, comparing DTVM multipass and lazy JIT against Wasmtime and Wasmer backends.
claimed_speedup: Paper (arXiv preprint, April 2025): average time-to-first-invocation speedup over Wasmtime (Cranelift) of 22.21x on 30 PolyBench cases and 18.87x on WAPM cases (0.95-0.96 ms vs 20.5-20.6 ms, up to 21.54x per case on PolyBench and 23.36x-24.51x on WAPM); 4.05x (Singlepass) to 234.13x (LLVM) over the Wasmer backends on PolyBench. PolyBench processing time (load + compile + execute): faster than Wasmtime (Cranelift) in 20 of 30 cases (1.20x average on those, 0.76x on the 10 it loses) and 11.03x-12.14x on average over the three Wasmer backends. Fibonacci(30): 11.73 ms, which is 11.8% less than Wasmtime (Cranelift), 25.6% less than Wasmer (Cranelift), 29.6% less than Wasmer (Singlepass) and 40.5% less than Wasmer (LLVM).
compiler_and_flags: Test programs: PolyBench/C 4.2.1 built with wasi-sdk clang -O3 -DSMALL_DATASET -DDATA_TYPE_IS_INT -DPOLYBENCH_DUMP_ARRAYS (benchmarks/paper/benchmarks/polybenchc/build.sh); DTVM built with cmake -DZEN_ENABLE_MULTIPASS_JIT=ON against LLVM 15; the CMake build type used for the paper runs is not stated. Baselines: paper used Wasmtime 31.0.0 and Wasmer 5.0.4/5.0.5; the reproduction package pins Wasmtime 45.0.0 and Wasmer 7.1.0.
hardware: Compute-optimized cloud VM, 8 vCPU, 16 GiB, Intel Xeon Platinum 8369B @ 2.70GHz, Turbo Boost off, CentOS 7.9 with Linux 3.10 (paper section 5)
tradeoffs: Built for blockchain smart contracts (deterministic execution, gas metering, EVM ABI compatibility, TEE portability), not a general-purpose WASI runtime. Lazy JIT with LLVM 15 requires x86-64; the singlepass JIT and interpreter modes are the portable ones. Small codebase (69.5 KLoC vs 143.6 KLoC for Wasmtime per the paper).
caveats: The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv 2504.16552), not peer reviewed. The reproduction package under benchmarks/paper ships cases, scripts and version pins but no result data, and its own notes say Wasmtime and Wasmer keep an on-disk module cache by default while DTVM recompiles on every launch, so wall-clock runs need the cache disabled; the contract microbenchmark runner is not included. The paper's runs used older Wasmtime and Wasmer versions (31.0.0, 5.0.x) than the package now pins (45.0.0, 7.1.0). Time-to-first-invocation compares DTVM's lazy per-function compile against baselines that compile the whole module eagerly. Wasmtime is faster than DTVM in 10 of 30 PolyBench cases (0.76x average there) and DTVM is slower than Wasmer Singlepass in one WAPM case. Host APIs are mocked in memory. Numbers read from the paper PDF checked into the repo (resources/DTVM_paper.pdf), fetched through the Git LFS media host.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/webassembly?l=c++ page 3 (DTVMStack/DTVM), then benchmarks/paper README and resources/DTVM_paper.pdf

name: WAMR iwasm (libsodium WebAssembly benchmark, 2022-12 edition)
workload: libsodium's built-in benchmark suite (61 crypto and utility tests) compiled once to WebAssembly and run on iwasm, Wasmtime, Wasmer (Cranelift, LLVM, Singlepass), WasmEdge, wazero, wasm2c, Node, Bun and wasm3, with native code as reference.
claimed_speedup: iwasm is faster than Wasmtime on all 61 common tests: geometric-mean time ratio 0.665 (about 1.5x faster, derived from page data), per-test ratio between 0.47 and 0.98. Against native its geometric-mean time is 2.30x, versus 3.46x for Wasmtime, 3.35x for WasmEdge and 3.91x for Node (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: The iwasm CSV does not say whether it ran the AOT compiler output (wamrc) or an interpreter; an interpreter cannot plausibly reach these times, so AOT is assumed. AOT needs a separate compile step and LLVM at build time; the fast interpreter and JIT modes trade this differently.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (is_evidence_for_known). The 2022-12 edition of jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks (archived, ISC licence) has no README: its res/ directory holds one CSV per runtime (test name;time) for the libsodium WebAssembly benchmark, and the commit log names no runtime versions, compiler flags or CPU, so tier B (independent suite, methodology incomplete). All ratios here are computed from the 61 tests present in every CSV (derived from page data); time units are not stated but lower is faster (native is the fastest row). The author's write-up of that edition is on a blocked blog and was not read. The 2021-Q1 edition of the same suite used LLVM 11.1.0 with wasm-opt -O4 on the shared wasm files and called each runtime through libsodium's wasi-test-wrapper.sh. The iwasm run mode and version are therefore inferred, not documented.
found_via: GitHub: jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks (listed by github.com/topics/webassembly-runtime), 2022-12/res/iwasm.csv against wasmtime.csv

name: wabt wasm2c (libsodium WebAssembly benchmark, 2022-12 edition)
workload: libsodium's built-in benchmark suite (61 crypto and utility tests) compiled once to WebAssembly, translated to C with wasm2c and built natively, versus the same wasm on Wasmtime, Wasmer, WasmEdge, iwasm, wazero, Node, Bun and wasm3.
claimed_speedup: wasm2c is faster than Wasmtime on 59 of 61 common tests: geometric-mean time ratio 0.684 (about 1.46x faster, derived from page data), per-test ratio between 0.43 and 1.43. Against native its geometric-mean time is 2.36x, versus 3.46x for Wasmtime and 2.89x for Wasmer (LLVM) (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: wasm2c output is a C source tree that must be built per module with a C compiler the user supplies. Not uniformly fast: on the first test row (aead_aegis128l) its time is about 74x native (derived from page data), and it is up to 1.43x slower than Wasmtime on some tests; the cause is not documented.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project (is_evidence_for_known). The 2022-12 edition of jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks (archived, ISC licence) has no README: its res/ directory holds one CSV per runtime (test name;time) for the libsodium WebAssembly benchmark, and the commit log names no runtime versions, compiler flags or CPU, so tier B (independent suite, methodology incomplete). All ratios here are computed from the 61 tests present in every CSV (derived from page data); time units are not stated but lower is faster (native is the fastest row). The author's write-up of that edition is on a blocked blog and was not read. The 2021-Q1 edition of the same suite used LLVM 11.1.0 with wasm-opt -O4 on the shared wasm files and called each runtime through libsodium's wasi-test-wrapper.sh. The C compiler and flags used to build the wasm2c output are not recorded in the repo.
